entry.title: SAP Business One Webhooks via Service Layer — Part 1: Concepts, Architecture, and Your First Webhook
entry.content:
Who This Series Is For

This series is written for SAP Business One partners and developers who build integrations on top of SAP Business One. You might be:

  • A developer building a custom add-on that needs to react in real time when SAP Business One data changes
  • A solution architect designing an integration between SAP Business One and a third-party system (e.g. a CRM, a logistics platform, a Power Automate flow)
  • A technical consultant who wants to understand what webhooks can do for your customers

You do not need to be an expert in SAP Business One internals. If you know what Service Layer is, know what a REST API is, and have some basic programming experience, you have everything you need to follow along.

Part 1 Overview

Part 1 is all about getting a solid foundation. We will cover:

  1. What polling is, why it is problematic, and what webhooks solve
  2. How the SAP Business One webhook architecture works, piece by piece
  3. What you need before you start
  4. Enabling webhooks for a company
  5. Exploring the Event Catalog
  6. Creating your very first webhook subscription
  7. The Handshake — what it is, why it matters, and how to implement it
  8. Receiving and validating your first notification

By the end of Part 1 you will have a working webhook that fires every time a sales order is created in SAP Business One, and you will understand exactly why every part of the setup exists.

 

1. The Problem: Polling Is Inefficient

Let's start with the problem webhooks solve, because understanding the problem is what makes the solution click.

What is polling?

Imagine you ordered a package online and you want to know when it arrives. One way to do it: walk to your front door every five minutes and check. That is polling — you repeatedly ask "has anything changed?"

In SAP Business One integrations, polling looks like this:

Every 60 seconds:
  GET /b1s/v2/Orders?$filter=UpdateDate ge '20261001'&$orderby=UpdateDate desc
  → if new orders found, process them
  → if nothing new, discard the response and wait 60 seconds

This works, but it has serious problems:

Problem

Explanation

Unnecessary load

You are making hundreds or thousands of API calls per day even when nothing has changed

Latency

If you poll every 60 seconds, you can be up to 60 seconds late reacting to an event

Complexity

You need to track watermarks (last-seen timestamps or IDs) to avoid re-processing the same records

Service Layer cost

Every poll is a real database query. Multiply this by many integrations across many companies

Rate limits

Heavy polling can hit Service Layer rate limits or degrade performance for other users

You can poll more frequently to reduce latency, but that makes the load problem worse. You cannot fully solve both at the same time.

What do webhooks solve?

Webhooks flip the model around. Instead of you repeatedly asking SAP Business One "did anything change?", SAP Business One tells you the moment something happens.

Back to the package analogy: instead of checking your door every five minutes, you install a smart doorbell that calls your phone the instant the package arrives. You do nothing until there is something to do.

In integration terms:

When an Order is Created in SAP Business One:
  SAP Business One sends HTTP POST to https://your-app.example.com/webhook
  → your app receives it instantly
  → your app processes it
  → done

No polling loop. No wasted calls. No latency beyond the network round-trip.

When should you still use polling instead of webhooks?

Webhooks are the right choice for most real-time integration scenarios, but polling still makes sense when:

  • You need to query historical data (e.g. "give me all orders from the last 3 months")
  • You are building a report or dashboard that aggregates data on demand
  • The event you care about is not in the SAP Business One Event Catalog (see Section 4)
  • You need to query complex data that requires joins or filters not expressible in webhook payloads

For everything else — reacting to business object changes in near-real-time — webhooks are the better tool.

 

2. How SAP Business One Webhook Architecture Works

Before writing a single line of code, you need a clear mental model of all the components involved and how they talk to each other.

Let's walk through each component.

SAP Business One Core

This is where business events originate. When a user creates a sales order through the SAP Business One Desktop Client, or a developer creates one via DI API, or someone uses the SAP Business One Web Client — the core records that transaction. Webhooks are triggered regardless of which channel created or modified the record. This is important: you get notifications for everything, not just Service Layer API calls.

Service Layer

Service Layer is the REST/OData gateway you already know. In the webhook context it plays two roles:

  1. API surface for webhook management: You create, read, update, and delete webhook subscriptions by calling EventSubscriptions endpoints through Service Layer.
  2. Event recorder: When SAP Business One Core processes a transaction that matches a subscription, Service Layer writes a record to the EventNotifications entity. This is your audit trail — you can query it at any time to see what was sent, when, and whether delivery succeeded.

Webhook Messenger Service

This is the new component introduced alongside webhook support. It is a background daemon (a system service, not a process you start manually) that runs on the SAP Business One server, listening on port 40008.

Its job is simple: pick up events, package them into HTTP POST requests, and send them to your endpoint. It handles:

  • Batching: Instead of firing one HTTP call per event, it can bundle multiple events into a single POST (configurable)
  • Retries: If your endpoint is down or slow, the Messenger retries with exponential backoff
  • Authentication: It adds the right headers (Basic, HMAC signature, OAuth Bearer) before sending
  • SSL: It verifies your endpoint's certificate (configurable)
  • Order guarantee: Within a single company, events are delivered in the order they occurred

You do not interact with the Messenger Service directly through code. You configure its behavior through Service Layer's CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo API, and you verify it is running using a simple telnet connectivity check.

Your Webhook Endpoint

This is the piece you build. It is an HTTPS URL that:

  1. Accepts GET requests (for the handshake, explained in Section 7)
  2. Accepts POST requests (for notifications)
  3. Returns HTTP 200 promptly when it has successfully received a request

That is really all it needs to do at a minimum. The actual processing of the notification — looking up related data, writing to your database, triggering a workflow — can happen synchronously or asynchronously, depending on your architecture.

3. Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have the following in place.

SAP Business One version

Webhooks require SAP Business One 10.0 FP 2602 or later. Some advanced features (filter expressions, richer payloads) require FP 2608 or later — these are clearly marked throughout this series.

Check your current version in the SAP Business One Desktop Client: Help → About SAP Business One.

Service Layer access

You need a working Service Layer installation and a user account that can call the API. Confirm this by making a simple call:

GET https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/$metadata

If you get a large XML response describing the OData schema, Service Layer is working.

An HTTPS endpoint

Your webhook URL must use HTTPS. Plain HTTP is not accepted. For production, this means:

  • A valid SSL certificate (from a trusted CA, or a self-signed one you import into the Messenger's trust store)
  • A publicly routable URL 

For development and testing, you have two good options:

Option A — webhook.site: Go to https://webhook.site, and you will get a unique temporary HTTPS URL instantly. Paste it as your WebhookURL. Every request it receives is shown in the browser in real time. Zero setup.

Option B — ngrok: If you want to run a real server on your laptop during development, install ngrok and run:

ngrok http 3000

This creates a public HTTPS tunnel to your local port 3000. Use the https://...ngrok.io URL as your WebhookURL.

User permissions

By default, only superusers can manage event subscriptions. If you are testing with a normal user account, ask your  administrator to grant the Webhook Manipulation permission (Permission ID 2249) to your user. We cover this in detail in Part 2.

4. Enable Webhooks for the Company

Webhooks are disabled by default for every company database. This is a deliberate choice — enabling webhooks activates the Messenger Service for that company, which has performance implications, so it should be a conscious opt-in.

Enable webhooks by calling CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo:

POST https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo

{
    "AdminInfo": {
        "EnableWebhook": "tYES"
    }
}

A successful response returns HTTP 204 (No Content).

Common error at this step

If you receive error 10001237 – Enter valid folder path, it means your company's admin info has folder paths (like ExcelFolderPath or XMLFileFolderPath) pointing to directories that either do not exist on the server or that the Service Layer service account cannot access.

The fix: include those paths in the same call and set them to empty strings or valid paths:

POST https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo

{
    "AdminInfo": {
        "EnableWebhook": "tYES",
        "ExcelFolderPath": "",
        "XMLFileFolderPath": ""
    }
}

This error is particularly common when the company database was migrated from another server and the folder paths were not updated.

Verify the current state

To check whether webhooks are currently enabled (and see all related settings), call:

GET https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/CompanyService_GetAdminInfo

Look for "EnableWebhook": "tYES" in the response. We cover all the other configuration fields in Part 2.

Note: By default, a company can have up to 16 webhook subscriptions. If you need more, increase MaxNumberOfWebHooks in the same CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo call. Part 2 covers the full set of configuration options.

5. Exploring the Event Catalog

Now that webhooks are enabled, you need to know what events you can subscribe to. The Event Catalog is the complete list.

GET https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/EventSubscriptionsService_GetEventCatalog

The response looks like this:

{
    "@odata.context": "...",
    "Version": "1.0",
    "Description": "SAP Business One Event Catalog",
    "value": [
        {
            "BusinessObject": "BusinessPartners",
            "ObjectType": "2",
            "TransactionTypes": "Created,Updated,Deleted"
        },
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Orders",
            "ObjectType": "17",
            "TransactionTypes": "Created,Updated,Deleted,Closed,Cancelled,Reopened"
        },
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Invoices",
            "ObjectType": "13",
            "TransactionTypes": "Created,Updated,Deleted,Closed,Cancelled"
        },
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Activities",
            "ObjectType": "1007",
            "TransactionTypes": "Created,Updated,Deleted"
        }
        ...
    ]
}

What BusinessObject values mean

The BusinessObject names in the catalog are exactly the entity names used in Service Layer. For example:

  • Orders → the Orders entity in Service Layer (/b1s/v2/Orders)
  • BusinessPartners → the BusinessPartners entity
  • Invoices → A/R Invoices

You can also subscribe to User-Defined Objects (UDOs) and User-Defined Tables (UDTs) — they appear in the catalog too if they exist in your company database.

Transaction types

Type

Meaning

Created

A new record was added

Updated

An existing record was modified

Deleted

A record was deleted

Closed

A document was closed (e.g. a fully delivered sales order)

Cancelled

A document was cancelled

Reopened

A previously closed document was reopened

Not every business object supports all transaction types. For example, BusinessPartners only supports Created, Updated, Deleted — you cannot cancel a business partner. The catalog tells you exactly which types apply to each object.

6. Creating Your First Webhook Subscription

An EventSubscription is the record that tells SAP Business One: "when event X happens, send a notification to URL Y". Let's create the simplest possible one.

The minimal subscription

POST https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions

{
    "WebhookID": "MyFirstWebhook",
    "WebhookURL": "https://webhook.site/your-unique-id",
    "AuthenticationType": "None",
    "Handshake": "tNO",
    "EventCollection": [
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Orders",
            "TransactionType": "Created"
        }
    ]
}

Let's explain every field:

WebhookID — A unique name you give this subscription within your company. Think of it as a primary key. It can be any string, as long as it is unique per company. Choose something descriptive: OrderCreatedWebhook, BPUpdateSync, etc.

WebhookURL — The HTTPS URL where SAP Business One will POST notifications. For this first test, paste your webhook.site URL here.

AuthenticationType — How SAP Business One authenticates when posting to your URL. We set it explicitly to "None" for now — note that the default is "HMAC", so always include this field if you want no authentication. Part 2 covers all authentication options in detail.

Handshake — Whether SAP Business One should verify your endpoint is reachable before creating the subscription. We set it to "tNO" to skip this for now. We will explain the handshake properly in Section 7.

EventCollection — The list of events to subscribe to. Each item has:

  • BusinessObject: which entity to watch
  • TransactionType: which operation to watch

A successful creation returns HTTP 201 Created along with the full subscription object, including system-assigned properties like State ("Active") and WorkMode ("Standard").

Testing it right away

After creating the subscription, go create a sales order — through the Desktop Client, Web Client, or via a Service Layer POST. Within moments, you should see a POST request arrive at your webhook.site URL. Click on it to see the payload. It will look something like this:

[
  {
    "id": "5ac18923-cfce-40d3-a31e-7154ca4d5191",
    "specversion": "1.0",
    "source": "/default/sap.b1/DEMODB1",
    "type": "sap.b1.Orders.Created.v1",
    "subject": "91",
    "time": "2025-11-10T23:10:22.917Z",
    "datacontenttype": "application/json",
    "data": {
      "DocEntry": "91"
    }
  }
]

Congratulations — you just received your first webhook notification from SAP Business One.

Understanding the notification payload

The payload follows the SAP Events specification (SAP's event notification standard, based on CloudEvents). Let's go through each field:

Field

Example value

What it means

id

"5ac18923-..."

A globally unique ID for this specific notification event. Use this for deduplication.

specversion

"1.0"

The SAP Events spec version. Always "1.0".

source

"/default/sap.b1/DEMODB1"

Identifies the SAP Business One system and company database that produced the event. Useful when one endpoint serves multiple companies.

type

"sap.b1.Orders.Created.v1"

The event type. Always formatted as sap.b1.{BusinessObject}.{Operation}.v1. Parse this to route events in your handler.

subject

"91"

The primary key of the affected record. For Orders, this is DocEntry. For BusinessPartners, it would be CardCode.

time

"2025-11-10T23:10:22.917Z"

UTC timestamp of when the event occurred.

datacontenttype

"application/json"

Always "application/json".

data

{"DocEntry": "91"}

The payload data — at minimum contains the key field(s) of the business object. Can include more fields if configured (see Part 3).

Important: The payload is always a JSON array, even when there is only one event. This is because the Messenger batches notifications — multiple events can arrive in a single HTTP POST. Always iterate over the array.

7. The Handshake: Verifying Your Endpoint

In the minimal example above we set "Handshake": "tNO" to skip verification. For real integrations, you should always use the handshake. Here is why — and how it works.

Why the handshake exists

Imagine someone gets hold of your credentials and creates a webhook subscription pointing to https://victim-company.example.com/some-endpoint. Without a handshake, SAP Business One would start sending potentially sensitive business data to an arbitrary URL.

The handshake is a proof of ownership mechanism: SAP Business One sends a challenge to your URL, and your URL must echo it back. This proves you control the endpoint before SAP Business One will accept the subscription or resume delivery.

It is similar to how services like Stripe, GitHub, or Slack verify webhook endpoints during configuration.

How the handshake works, step by step

When a handshake is triggered, SAP Business One sends a GET request to your WebhookURL:

Step 1: SAP Business One generates a random token (e.g. "abc123xyz")

Step 2: SAP Business One sends a GET request:
  GET https://your-app.example.com/webhook/orders
  X-B1-Webhook-Token: abc123xyz

Step 3: Your endpoint reads the X-B1-Webhook-Token header
        and returns the token in the response body:
  HTTP 200
  Content-Type: application/json
  {"Challenge": "abc123xyz"}

Step 4: SAP Business One reads the response body, extracts "Challenge",
        and compares it to the token it sent.
        If they match → handshake successful.
        If they don't match (or the request times out) → handshake fails.

When is the handshake triggered?

The handshake is triggered automatically in two situations:

  1. When creating a subscription with "Handshake": "tYES" — if the handshake fails, the subscription is not created and you get an error. This is a safety guard.
  2. When resuming a subscription that has "Handshake": "tYES" — SAP Business One re-verifies your endpoint is up before re-activating delivery.

You can also trigger it manually at any time:

POST https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('MyFirstWebhook')/Handshake

This is useful when you want to verify your endpoint is correctly configured without waiting for an event to occur.

Implementing the handshake in your endpoint

Your endpoint needs to respond to both GET (handshake) and POST (notification delivery) requests. Here is a simple Node.js/Express implementation:

const express = require('express');
const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

// Handle both handshake (GET) and notifications (POST) on the same route
app.all('/webhook/orders', (req, res) => {

    if (req.method === 'GET') {
        // ── Handshake handler ──────────────────────────────────────────
        const token = req.headers['x-b1-webhook-token'];

        if (!token) {
            // Not a handshake request — could be a health check or browser visit
            return res.status(200).send('Webhook endpoint is running.');
        }

        // Echo the token back as the "Challenge"
        console.log(`Handshake received. Token: ${token}`);
        return res.status(200).json({ Challenge: token });
    }

    if (req.method === 'POST') {
        // ── Notification handler ───────────────────────────────────────
        // We'll fill this in properly in the next section
        console.log('Notification received:', JSON.stringify(req.body, null, 2));
        return res.sendStatus(200);
    }

    // Reject anything else
    return res.status(405).send('Method Not Allowed');
});

app.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log('Webhook endpoint running on http://localhost:3000');
    console.log('Use ngrok or similar to expose this over HTTPS for testing');
});

What if the handshake fails?

If the handshake fails during subscription creation, you will receive an error response with a message indicating the failure reason, for example:

{
    "error": {
        "code": "<error-code>",
        "message": {
            "value": "Webhook handshake error."
        }
    }
}

Common reasons:

  • Your endpoint is not reachable from the SAP Business One server (firewall, wrong URL, service not running)
  • Your endpoint does not respond to GET requests (only POST)
  • Your endpoint does not return the Challenge field in the response body
  • Your endpoint takes more than 10 seconds to respond (the default timeout)
  • SSL certificate issues (invalid, expired, or self-signed with no import)

Creating a subscription WITH handshake

Now let's create a proper subscription with the handshake enabled:

POST https://{your-server}:50000/b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions

{
    "WebhookID": "OrderCreatedWebhook",
    "WebhookURL": "https://your-app.example.com/webhook/orders",
    "AuthenticationType": "None",
    "Handshake": "tYES",
    "VerifyCertificate": "tYES",
    "EventCollection": [
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Orders",
            "TransactionType": "Created"
        }
    ]
}

If your endpoint correctly handles the handshake GET request, the subscription is created and delivery begins immediately.

8. Receiving Notifications: A Working Example

Now let's build a runnable webhook endpoint that handles both the handshake and event notifications, and processes the events properly.

What your endpoint needs to do

When a notification arrives, your endpoint needs to:

  1. Accept the POST request
  2. Read the JSON body (array of event objects)
  3. Iterate over the events
  4. Return HTTP 200 quickly (before doing heavy processing)
  5. Process the events (look up data, write to your DB, trigger downstream actions)

Returning HTTP 200 quickly is important. The Webhook Messenger has a 10-second timeout (configurable). If your endpoint takes longer than that to respond, the Messenger considers the delivery failed and schedules a retry. You do not want retries caused by slow processing — separate receiving from processing.

A Node.js code snippet

const express = require('express');
const app = express();

app.use(express.json());

// ─── Simple in-memory store to demonstrate idempotency ────────────────────────
// In production, use a database or Redis
const processedEventIds = new Set();

// ─── Webhook route ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
app.all('/webhook/orders', (req, res) => {

    // ── Handshake (GET) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    if (req.method === 'GET') {
        const token = req.headers['x-b1-webhook-token'];
        if (!token) {
            return res.status(200).send('Webhook endpoint is running.');
        }
        console.log(`[Handshake] Token received: ${token}`);
        return res.status(200).json({ Challenge: token });
    }

    // ── Notification delivery (POST) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    if (req.method === 'POST') {
        const events = req.body;

        // Validate the payload is an array
        if (!Array.isArray(events)) {
            console.error('[Error] Unexpected payload shape — expected an array');
            return res.status(400).send('Bad Request');
        }

        // Acknowledge receipt immediately — do not do heavy processing here
        // This prevents the Messenger from timing out and retrying
        res.sendStatus(200);

        // Process events asynchronously after responding
        setImmediate(() => processEvents(events));

        return;
    }

    res.status(405).send('Method Not Allowed');
});

// ─── Event processing logic ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function processEvents(events) {
    for (const event of events) {
        const eventId = event.id;

        // Idempotency check: skip if we already processed this event
        // This protects against duplicate deliveries caused by retries
        if (processedEventIds.has(eventId)) {
            console.log(`[Skip] Already processed event: ${eventId}`);
            continue;
        }

        // Mark as processed before doing work
        // (prevents concurrent duplicate processing in multi-threaded environments)
        processedEventIds.add(eventId);

        console.log(`[Processing] Event: ${event.type}`);
        console.log(`  Source: ${event.source}`);
        console.log(`  Subject (DocEntry): ${event.subject}`);
        console.log(`  Time: ${event.time}`);
        console.log(`  Data: ${JSON.stringify(event.data)}`);

        try {
            await handleEvent(event);
        } catch (err) {
            console.error(`[Error] Failed to handle event ${eventId}:`, err.message);
            // Log and continue — do not let one bad event block the rest of the batch
        }
    }
}

// ─── Business logic ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
async function handleEvent(event) {
    // Route by event type
    if (event.type === 'sap.b1.Orders.Created.v1') {
        const docEntry = event.data.DocEntry;
        console.log(`[Handler] New order created: DocEntry = ${docEntry}`);

        // Here you would typically:
        // 1. Call Service Layer to get the full order details:
        //    GET /b1s/v2/Orders(${docEntry})
        // 2. Transform or enrich the data
        // 3. Push to your system (CRM, warehouse, etc.)
    }
    // Add more handlers as needed...
}

// ─── Start server ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
app.listen(3000, () => {
    console.log('Webhook server listening on port 3000');
});

Key patterns in this example

Respond before processing. We call res.sendStatus(200) first, then use setImmediate() to run the actual processing outside the request handler. This pattern prevents the Messenger from timing out if processing takes more than a few seconds.

Idempotency. We check processedEventIds before processing each event. The Messenger can deliver the same event more than once (e.g. if your server returned 200 but then crashed, or if a retry fired before the first response arrived). Using the unique event.id field to deduplicate protects you from processing the same order creation twice. In production, replace the in-memory Set with a database table or Redis.

Error isolation. The try/catch inside the loop means a single failing event does not abort the rest of the batch.

Type-based routing. Parsing event.type lets a single endpoint handle events from multiple business objects. Alternatively, you can create separate WebhookURL values per subscription.

9. Verifying the Webhook Messenger Is Running

If your endpoint is set up correctly but no notifications are arriving, the first thing to check is whether the Webhook Messenger Service is reachable.

telnet {your-b1-server} 40008

If the connection succeeds, you will see:

Trying {your-b1-server}...
Connected to {your-b1-server}.
Escape character is '^]'.
SAP Business One Webhook Messenger

If the connection is refused or times out, the Messenger Service is either not running or blocked by a firewall. Contact your SAP Business One system administrator to:

  1. Verify the Webhook Messenger Service is installed and started (it is a separate installable component)
  2. Open port 40008 in the firewall between the Messenger and your endpoint

Part 1 Summary

You now have a solid foundation:

What you learned

Why it matters

Polling vs webhooks

Know when to use each and why webhooks are more efficient

SAP Business One webhook architecture

Understand what each component does so you can troubleshoot problems

Enabling webhooks

First step for any company database

Event Catalog

Know what events are available before designing your subscription

Creating a subscription

The core API call with all fields explained

Handshake mechanism

Security verification that proves you own the endpoint

Notification payload

Parse type, subject, data, and id correctly

Idempotent processing

Essential pattern for handling retries without duplicating work

What's Next

Part 2 covers everything about managing subscriptions over time, all four authentication methods (None, Basic, HMAC, OAuth) in depth, monitoring and querying EventNotifications, the pause/resume/replay lifecycle, and how to tune the configuration settings for your production environment.

Part 3 covers advanced topics: filter expressions to only receive relevant notifications, richer payloads with BizObjProps, the full webhook formula reference, and a comprehensive production best-practices guide.

entry.title: SAP Business One Webhooks via Service Layer — Part 2: Managing Event Subscription and Notification
entry.content:
Introduction

In Part 1, we created a minimal webhook subscription and received our first notification. That is enough to get something working, but a production integration requires much more:

  • How do you change what events a subscription listens to, without deleting and recreating it?
  • How do you make sure only SAP Business One — and not an attacker — can post to your endpoint?
  • How do you know if a notification was delivered successfully?
  • What happens when your endpoint goes down, and how do you recover?
  • How do you tune the system for high-volume production scenarios?

This part answers all of those questions.

1. Managing Event Subscriptions

Retrieve all subscriptions

To see all webhooks configured for the current company:

GET /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions

The response is an OData collection. You can use standard OData query options:

# Get only active subscriptions
GET /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions?$filter=State eq 'Active'

# Get subscriptions using HMAC authentication
GET /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions?$filter=AuthenticationType eq 'HMAC'

# Get specific fields only
GET /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions?$select=WebhookID,WebhookURL,State,WorkMode

Retrieve a specific subscription

GET /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')

You will get back the full subscription object, including current State and WorkMode — which change over the subscription's lifecycle.

Update a subscription

Subscriptions are updated with HTTP PATCH (partial update — only fields you include are changed).

Note: WebhookID and WebhookURL are immutable — they cannot be changed after the subscription is created. If you need to change the endpoint URL, delete the subscription and create a new one.

For example, to disable certificate verification on an existing subscription:

PATCH /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')

{
    "VerifyCertificate": "tNO"
}

This example only changes VerifyCertificate. Everything else (auth, events, handshake settings) stays the same.

Adding events to a subscription

By default, PATCH appends to the EventCollection. So to add "Invoices Created" to a subscription that already watches "Orders Created":

PATCH /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')

{
    "EventCollection": [
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Invoices",
            "TransactionType": "Created"
        }
    ]
}

After this PATCH, the subscription watches both Orders.Created and Invoices.Created. The existing Orders.Created entry was not touched.

Replacing the event list entirely

If you want to remove an event (or do a clean replacement), use the B1S-ReplaceCollectionsOnPatch header. When this header is true, the EventCollection you provide in the PATCH replaces the entire existing collection rather than appending.

Example: we want to keep Invoices.Created but remove Orders.Created:

PATCH /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')
B1S-ReplaceCollectionsOnPatch: true

{
    "EventCollection": [
        {
            "BusinessObject": "Invoices",
            "TransactionType": "Created"
        }
    ]
}

After this, the subscription only watches Invoices.Created. The previous Orders.Created entry is gone.

This header is not specific to webhooks — it is a general Service Layer convention for replacing collections on PATCH operations.

Delete a subscription

Note: Only subscriptions in Inactive state can be deleted. If the subscription is currently Active, pause it first (see The Subscription Lifecycle ) before deleting.

DELETE /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')

Returns HTTP 204 on success. Previously dispatched notifications in EventNotifications are not deleted.

2. Understanding Subscription States

Every subscription has a State property that reflects its current health:

State

Meaning

What to do

Active

Healthy. Notifications are being delivered normally.

Nothing required.

Inactive

Manually paused (via the Pause API), or deactivated by the system after too many delivery failures.

Investigate and fix the root cause, then call Resume.

Exceptional

The Messenger is encountering delivery failures but has not yet exhausted all retry attempts. The system is actively retrying.

Monitor. If retries succeed, state returns to Active. If all retries exhaust, state moves to Inactive.

Think of Exceptional as a yellow warning light — something is wrong but the system is still trying to fix it. Inactive is the red light — the system gave up, and you need to intervene.

3. The Subscription Lifecycle: Pause, Resume, and Replay

Pausing a subscription

Pausing is useful during planned maintenance of your endpoint. Instead of deleting and recreating the subscription, you pause it:

POST /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')/Pause

Returns HTTP 204. The subscription moves to Inactive state. Events that occur while paused are still recorded in EventNotifications, but are not delivered to your endpoint.

Resuming a subscription

When your endpoint is back online:

POST /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')/Resume

Returns HTTP 204. If Handshake is "tYES", the handshake is performed again before re-activating. This ensures your endpoint is genuinely back up before the Messenger starts sending again.

What about events missed during downtime?

By default, events that occurred while your subscription was Inactive are lost — they will not be automatically re-delivered when you resume. The Messenger's standard mode (WorkMode: Standard) only sends new events going forward.

This is where Replay comes in.

Replaying missed notifications

If your endpoint was down for a period of time and you need to catch up on the events that occurred during that window, use the Replay API:

POST /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')/Replay

Prerequisites for replay:

  • The subscription must currently be in Inactive state
  • The subscription must have "Handshake": "tYES"
  • The Messenger performs a handshake before starting the replay, to confirm your endpoint is ready

What replay does:

  1. The subscription's WorkMode changes to "Replay"
  2. The Messenger re-sends all notifications from EventNotifications that occurred after the last successful delivery timestamp
  3. Once all missed notifications are delivered, WorkMode automatically reverts to "Standard" and normal processing resumes

Important side effect of replay: During the replay operation, the Messenger pauses delivery to all other active webhooks for the same company, until the replay is complete. This ensures ordering — replayed events for your webhook are delivered before any new events are sent to other webhooks.

This side effect has a practical implication: if your company has many webhooks and your missed window was very large, replay could block other webhooks for a long time. Design your endpoint for high availability (load balancing, health checks, auto-restart) to minimize the frequency of needing replay.

4. Authentication: Securing Your Webhook Endpoint

Authentication answers a critical question: how does your endpoint know that a POST request genuinely came from SAP Business One, and not from an attacker who discovered your webhook URL?

Without authentication, anyone who knows your URL can send fake events to your system. The Webhook Messenger supports four authentication types.

Authentication Type: None

"AuthenticationType": "None"

No authentication headers are added to the request. The Messenger posts to your URL with no credential.

When to use: Only for local development or demo environments where the URL is not publicly accessible. Never use in production.

Authentication Type: Basic

"AuthenticationType": "Basic",
"AuthenticationCred": "{\"Username\": \"webhookuser\", \"Password\": \"s3cr3tP@ssw0rd\"}"

The Messenger adds an HTTP Basic Authentication header to every request:

Authorization: Basic base64(webhookuser:s3cr3tP@ssw0rd)

Your endpoint checks this header. If it is missing or incorrect, return HTTP 401 Unauthorized — the Messenger will treat this as a failed delivery and retry.

Implementing Basic auth in Express (Node.js):

function checkBasicAuth(req, res, next) {
    const authHeader = req.headers['authorization'];
    if (!authHeader || !authHeader.startsWith('Basic ')) {
        return res.status(401).send('Missing Authorization header');
    }

    const base64Credentials = authHeader.slice(6);
    const credentials = Buffer.from(base64Credentials, 'base64').toString('utf8');
    const [username, password] = credentials.split(':');

    if (username !== 'webhookuser' || password !== 's3cr3tP@ssw0rd') {
        return res.status(401).send('Invalid credentials');
    }

    next();
}

app.post('/webhook/orders', checkBasicAuth, (req, res) => {
    // ... process notification
});

AuthenticationCred format for Basic:

The value is a JSON string (a string that, when parsed, produces a JSON object). Note the escaped quotes:

"AuthenticationCred": "{\"Username\": \"webhookuser\", \"Password\": \"s3cr3tP@ssw0rd\"}"

When to use: When you want simple authentication without the complexity of HMAC or OAuth. Better than nothing, but HMAC is more secure because the password is never sent in plain text (only Base64-encoded, which is easily decoded).

Authentication Type: HMAC (Recommended)

HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) is the most recommended approach for webhook security. Instead of sending a password, SAP Business One computes a cryptographic signature of the request (or the handshake token) using a shared secret key, and sends that signature as a header. Your endpoint recomputes the same signature and compares — if they match, the request is genuine.

"AuthenticationType": "HMAC",
"AuthenticationCred": "{\"Key\": \"your-base64-encoded-secret-key\", \"Algorithm\": \"HMACSha256\"}"

Supported algorithms: HMACSha256, HMACSha384, HMACSha512

Generating a good secret key:

# Generate a random 32-byte key and Base64-encode it
openssl rand -base64 32

Example output: i1mGRbx8DaYZQ6p7RJywYD1IauI+HyTj4TjyKSYv8sI=

Use this as your Key value.

What the Messenger sends:

For notification delivery:

POST https://your-app.example.com/webhook/orders
X-B1-Webhook-Signature: <HMAC-SHA256 of request body using your secret key>
Content-Type: application/json

[{...event payload...}]

For the handshake:

GET https://your-app.example.com/webhook/orders
X-B1-Webhook-Token: <random-token>
X-B1-Webhook-Signature: <HMAC-SHA256 of the token using your secret key>

Implementing HMAC verification in Node.js:

const crypto = require('crypto');

// Your secret key — load from environment variable, not hardcoded
const SECRET_KEY = Buffer.from(process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY, 'base64');

function verifyHmacSignature(payload, receivedSignature) {
    // Compute expected signature
    const expectedSignature = crypto
        .createHmac('sha256', SECRET_KEY)
        .update(payload)  // payload is the raw request body as a string
        .digest('base64');

    // Use timingSafeEqual to prevent timing attacks
    try {
        return crypto.timingSafeEqual(
            Buffer.from(receivedSignature, 'base64'),
            Buffer.from(expectedSignature, 'base64')
        );
    } catch {
        return false;
    }
}

// Middleware to capture raw body (needed for HMAC verification)
app.use(express.json({
    verify: (req, res, buf) => {
        req.rawBody = buf.toString('utf8');
    }
}));

app.all('/webhook/orders', (req, res) => {

    // ── Handshake (GET) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    if (req.method === 'GET') {
        const token = req.headers['x-b1-webhook-token'];
        if (!token) return res.status(200).send('Endpoint is running.');

        // Verify the HMAC signature on the handshake token
        const signature = req.headers['x-b1-webhook-signature'];
        if (signature) {
            if (!verifyHmacSignature(token, signature)) {
                console.error('[Handshake] HMAC verification failed');
                return res.status(401).send('Invalid signature');
            }
        }

        console.log('[Handshake] Verified. Echoing challenge.');
        return res.status(200).json({ Challenge: token });
    }

    // ── Notification (POST) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    if (req.method === 'POST') {
        const signature = req.headers['x-b1-webhook-signature'];

        if (!signature) {
            console.error('[Auth] Missing X-B1-Webhook-Signature header');
            return res.status(401).send('Missing signature');
        }

        if (!verifyHmacSignature(req.rawBody, signature)) {
            console.error('[Auth] HMAC signature mismatch');
            return res.status(401).send('Invalid signature');
        }

        // Signature verified — safe to process
        res.sendStatus(200);
        setImmediate(() => processEvents(req.body));
        return;
    }

    res.status(405).send('Method Not Allowed');
});

Why HMAC is better than Basic:

  • The secret key is never transmitted over the network (only the signature is)
  • Each request has a unique signature because it is derived from the request body
  • Even if an attacker intercepts one request, they cannot forge future ones without the key
  • You can rotate the key (update the AuthenticationCred on the subscription) without downtime

Authentication Type: OAuth (Client Credentials)

OAuth is the right choice when your endpoint is protected by an identity provider (like Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, or SAP BTP) and requires a Bearer token.

"AuthenticationType": "OAuth",
"AuthenticationCred": "{\"token_endpoint\": \"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token\", \"client_id\": \"your-client-id\", \"client_secret\": \"your-client-secret\", \"grant_type\": \"client_credentials\"}"

How it works:

Before sending each batch of notifications, the Webhook Messenger:

  1. Calls your token_endpoint with client_id, client_secret, and grant_type=client_credentials
  2. Receives an access token
  3. Adds Authorization: Bearer <access_token> to the notification request

The Messenger automatically refreshes the token when it expires, so you do not need to manage token lifecycle.

AuthenticationCred format for OAuth:

{
    "token_endpoint": "https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token",
    "client_id": "xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
    "client_secret": "your-client-secret-value",
    "grant_type": "client_credentials"
}

As a JSON string (what you pass to the API):

"{\"token_endpoint\": \"https://...\", \"client_id\": \"...\", \"client_secret\": \"...\", \"grant_type\": \"client_credentials\"}"

When to use: When your organisation already has an OAuth infrastructure and your endpoint is part of that ecosystem. Common in enterprise SAP BTP scenarios.

Authentication and the handshake together

When both handshake and authentication are configured, the handshake request includes the same authentication as regular notifications:

AuthenticationType

Handshake GET request headers

None

Only X-B1-Webhook-Token

Basic

X-B1-Webhook-Token + Authorization: Basic ...

HMAC

X-B1-Webhook-Token + X-B1-Webhook-Signature (HMAC of the token)

OAuth

X-B1-Webhook-Token + Authorization: Bearer <token>

This means your handshake handler also needs to verify the authentication header, which is why the HMAC example above checks x-b1-webhook-signature during the handshake.

5. Permission Control

By default, only superusers can create, read, update, or delete event subscriptions. Regular users attempting to do so get:

{
    "error": {
        "code": -6006,
        "message": {
            "lang": "en-us",
            "value": "You are not permitted to perform this action"
        }
    }
}

Granting permission through the SAP Business One client

  1. Log in to the SAP Business One Desktop Client as a superuser
  2. Go to Administration → System Initialization → Authorizations → General Authorizations
  3. Select the user you want to grant access to
  4. Search for "Webhook Manipulation" in the permission tree
  5. Change No Authorization to either:
    • Full Authorization — can create, read, update, delete
    • Read-Only — can only view subscriptions

Granting permission programmatically

You can also set this via Service Layer API (requires superuser credentials):

POST /b1s/v2/SBOBobService_SetSystemPermission

{
    "PermissionID": "2249",
    "UserCode": "user1",
    "Permission": 1
}

The Permission values:

Value

Meaning

1

Full Authorization (Read/Write)

2

Read Only

3

No Authorization

Permission ID 2249 is the fixed ID for "Webhook Manipulation" across all SAP Business One installations.

Important: Due to an internal permission cache, changes may take up to one minute to take effect. If you grant permission and immediately try to create a subscription, you may still get a 403. Wait a moment and try again.

6. Monitoring with EventNotifications

Every notification dispatched by the Webhook Messenger is also saved to the EventNotifications entity. This gives you a permanent, queryable audit trail — you can see exactly what was sent, when, to which webhooks, and whether delivery succeeded.

This is extremely valuable for:

  • Debugging delivery failures
  • Auditing which events triggered notifications
  • Checking the delivery status of a specific event
  • Understanding why a downstream system did not receive an event

The EventNotifications entity

EventNotifications is read-only — you can query it, but you cannot create, update, or delete records. The records are managed entirely by the SAP Business One Core and Webhook Messenger.

Key properties explained

EventID — A unique GUID identifying this event notification. This is the same id you see in the notification payload your endpoint receives. Use it to correlate what SAP Business One sent with what your endpoint received.

SourceDB — The company database where the event occurred. Important when one Messenger serves multiple companies.

BusinessObject — The entity that triggered the event (e.g. "Orders", "BusinessPartners").

Operation — What happened: Created, Updated, Deleted, Closed, Cancelled, Reopened.

Status — The delivery status:

Status

Meaning

New

The event was recorded but the Messenger has not yet attempted delivery

Delivered

Successfully delivered to all subscribed webhook endpoints

PartiallyDelivered

Delivered to some webhook endpoints but failed for others

Failed

All delivery attempts failed — no subscribers received it

Archived

The event was generated but all subscribed webhooks were inactive at the time, so no delivery was attempted

ReplayState — Whether this notification is part of a replay operation:

ReplayState

Meaning

None

Normal — not part of any replay

Replaying

Currently being replayed

Completed

Successfully replayed

FieldNames and FieldValues — The key fields of the affected record. For Orders, FieldNames is "DocEntry" and FieldValues is the DocEntry number (e.g. "91"). For BusinessPartners, FieldNames is "CardCode". For records with composite keys (like SpecialPrices), values are tab-separated.

CreateDate and CreateTime — When the event was recorded. Note: CreateDate stores the date with time zeroed out (2025-11-19T00:00:00Z), and CreateTime is a separate string in HH:mm:ss.fff format.

KeyData (FP 2608+) — The primary key data in a cleaner JSON format. For Orders:

{"DocEntry": 91}

For BusinessPartners:

{"CardCode": "C20000"}

For business objects with composite keys (e.g. SpecialPrices😞

{"CardCode": "C20000", "ItemCode": "I00001"}

Useful EventNotifications queries

Check recent delivery failures:

GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications?$filter=Status eq 'Failed'&$orderby=CreateDate desc,CreateTime desc&$top=20

Find notifications for a specific order:

GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications?$filter=BusinessObject eq 'Orders' and FieldValues eq '91'

Check all events from a specific date:

GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications?$filter=CreateDate ge '{YYYY-MM-DD}T00:00:00Z'&$orderby=CreateTime desc

Find all partially delivered notifications (some webhooks failed):

GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications?$filter=Status eq 'PartiallyDelivered'&$top=50

Get a specific notification by EventID:

GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications('3f03e9da-8dd6-4601-be18-5cad6790bfd3')

Building a simple monitoring dashboard

Using EventNotifications, you can build a live monitoring view for your integration:

# Overall delivery health by status
GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications?$apply=groupby((Status),aggregate($count as Count))

# Delivery failures per business object on a specific date
GET /b1s/v2/EventNotifications?$filter=Status eq 'Failed' and CreateDate ge '{YYYY-MM-DD}T00:00:00Z'&$apply=groupby((BusinessObject,Operation),aggregate($count as Count))

7. The Retry Policy: What Happens When Delivery Fails

Understanding the retry policy helps you design your endpoint correctly and set realistic recovery expectations.

When does the Messenger retry?

The Messenger retries when your endpoint returns:

  • 5xx errors: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout
  • 408 Request Timeout
  • 429 Too Many Requests
  • Network-level failures: connection timeout, connection refused, DNS resolution failure

The Messenger does not retry for:

  • 2xx: Delivery succeeded
  • 4xx (except 408 and 429): These indicate a client error (bad request, auth failure, not found) — retrying would not help, so the Messenger marks the delivery as failed immediately
  • 3xx: Redirects are not followed

The retry schedule

The default configuration retries up to 3 times with a fixed interval of 2 seconds between each attempt:

Attempt

Delay before this attempt

Cumulative wait

Initial

0s

0s

Retry 1

2s

2s

Retry 2

2s

4s

Retry 3

2s

6s

If all attempts fail, the notification is marked Failed in EventNotifications. The subscription state transitions to Exceptional. If the subscription continues to fail across multiple events, it eventually moves to Inactive.

You can adjust the retry count and interval in the configuration settings (Section 9).

Designing your endpoint for retries

Return 200 quickly. The Messenger counts time from sending the request until receiving the response. If your endpoint takes longer than the configured WebhookRequestTimeout to process and respond, the Messenger sees a timeout and retries — even though you successfully processed the event. This leads to duplicate processing.

The correct pattern: respond with 200 immediately upon receipt, then process asynchronously. This is why Part 1's code example uses setImmediate() to defer processing.

Be idempotent. A retry delivers the same event again. Your handler must tolerate receiving the same event.id more than once. Use the id field as a deduplicate key in your database.

Return the right status codes. If you return 500 because of a temporary issue in your system (e.g. DB connection failed), the Messenger will retry — that is the right behavior. If you return 400 because of a permanent problem (e.g. you cannot parse the payload), the Messenger will not retry — which is also correct, since retrying would not fix a parsing error. Use status codes semantically.

8. SSL Certificates

Webhook delivery is HTTPS-only. The Messenger validates the SSL certificate of your endpoint URL by default ("VerifyCertificate": "tYES").

Common SSL-related issues

Self-signed certificates: If your endpoint uses a self-signed certificate, the Messenger will reject it unless you import it into the Messenger's trusted certificate store.

Use the certificate import tool that ships with the Webhook Messenger installation. It is located at:

  • Windows: C:\Program Files\SAP\SAP Business One Webhook Messenger\tools\
  • Linux: Check the installation directory — typically under /opt/sap/...

Run the tool with --help for usage instructions. You need to run it as a system administrator.

Certificates from non-trusted CAs: Same solution as self-signed — import the CA certificate.

IP address in the URL: If your WebhookURL uses an IP address (e.g. https://192.168.1.100/webhook), the SSL certificate must include that IP address in its Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field. A certificate issued for example.com will not satisfy a URL using a raw IP address, even if the certificate is otherwise valid.

Bypassing certificate verification for development:

In development environments where you control the network, you can disable certificate verification:

PATCH /b1s/v2/EventSubscriptions('OrderCreatedWebhook')

{
    "VerifyCertificate": "tNO"
}

Never do this in production. Without certificate verification, a man-in-the-middle attacker could intercept your SAP Business One notifications.

9. Configuration Settings

The Webhook Messenger's behavior is configured at the company level via CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo. Here is every setting, with guidance on when and why to change the default.

Reading current settings

GET /b1s/v2/CompanyService_GetAdminInfo

Look for the webhook-related properties in the response.

Updating settings

POST /b1s/v2/CompanyService_UpdateAdminInfo

{
    "AdminInfo": {
        "MaxNumberOfWebHooks": 20,
        "WebhookRetryTimes": 5,
        "WebhookRetryInterval": 3,
        "WebhookRequestTimeout": 15,
        "MessageBatchLimit": 64,
        "MessageTTL": 48,
        "MessageRetentionTime": 60
    }
}

You can update as many or as few settings as you like in one call.

EnableWebhook (default: "tNO")

Enable or disable the entire webhook feature for the company. Set once during setup. No reason to change it after that unless you are decommissioning webhooks.

MaxNumberOfWebHooks (default: 16)

Maximum number of EventSubscription records that can exist for this company. If you try to create a 17th subscription when the default is 16, the API returns an error.

When to change: If your integration design requires more than 16 distinct webhook endpoints. For example, if you have one webhook per downstream system and you serve many systems. Increase thoughtfully — each additional webhook adds delivery load.

MessageTTL (default: 24 hours)

Time-to-live for webhook messages in the Messenger's queue. If a message sits in the queue for longer than this value without being delivered, it is discarded.

When to change: If your endpoint experiences extended outages (longer than 24 hours), increase this so messages are not discarded before your endpoint comes back. Keep it less than MessageRetentionTime.

Relationship with MessageRetentionTime: MessageTTL is the delivery window. MessageRetentionTime is how long the record stays in EventNotifications. TTL should always be significantly shorter than retention time.

WebhookRetryTimes (default: 3)

How many times to retry a failed delivery before giving up. 0 means no retries — first failure = permanent failure.

When to change:

  • Increase (e.g. to 5) if your endpoint is occasionally slow or returns transient errors and you want more chances before marking as failed
  • Decrease (e.g. to 1 or 0) if your endpoint is expected to be highly available and a failure should immediately be treated as a serious problem — fewer retries means faster failure detection

WebhookRetryInterval (default: 2 seconds)

The fixed interval in seconds between retry attempts. With the default of 2, each retry waits exactly 2 seconds after the previous failure.

When to change: Increase if your endpoint is known to need longer recovery time (e.g. it restarts slowly). Decrease if you want faster retry cycles.

WebhookRequestTimeout (default: 10 seconds)

How long the Messenger waits for a response from your endpoint before treating the request as timed out.

When to change: Increase if your endpoint is legitimately slow to respond due to network distance or infrastructure constraints. However, the better solution is to make your endpoint respond immediately (HTTP 200) and process asynchronously. Only increase the timeout as a last resort.

Minimum recommendation: Keep this at least 5 seconds to account for network latency.

MessageBatchLimit (default: 1024)

The maximum number of events bundled into a single HTTP POST to your endpoint.

When to change:

  • Decrease if your endpoint has payload size limits (e.g. an API gateway with a 1 MB body limit). If 1024 events × average event size exceeds your limit, reduce this
  • Decrease if you want near-real-time delivery with minimal batching (e.g. set to 1 for one event per POST — highest latency sensitivity, highest HTTP call volume)
  • Keep at default or increase if you are optimizing for throughput and your endpoint handles large batches well

Memory consideration: All batched events are held in the Messenger's memory queue. If your endpoint is slow and events accumulate, the queue fills up. The Messenger handles queue-full situations gracefully (waits for space), but sustained overload will cause delivery latency to grow.

MessageRetentionTime (default: 30 days)

How long EventNotification records are kept in the system before automatic deletion.

When to change:

  • Increase for compliance or audit requirements that mandate longer event history
  • Decrease to manage database storage, especially for high-volume event systems
  • Must be greater than MessageTTL

Part 2 Summary

You now have everything you need to build, secure, and operate a robust webhook integration:

What you learned

Why it matters

Full CRUD on subscriptions

Update without deleting; append or replace event lists

Subscription states (Active/Inactive/Exceptional)

Know when intervention is needed

Pause / Resume / Replay

Handle planned maintenance and unplanned downtime gracefully

Four authentication types

Choose the right security model; HMAC is recommended

Permission control

Grant access to non-superusers safely

EventNotifications entity

Query delivery history for monitoring and debugging

Retry policy and fixed-interval retries

Design idempotent endpoints; use status codes correctly

SSL certificate handling

Avoid certificate errors in production

All configuration settings

Tune for your specific throughput, latency, and reliability requirements

What's Next

Part 3 covers the advanced features introduced in FP 2608: filter expressions to reduce unwanted notifications, richer payloads with extra fields in the notification body, the full webhook formula language reference, and a comprehensive production readiness guide covering high availability, idempotency patterns, and operations runbook.
